title: Login with OIDC, sessions and tokens
tagline: Let an identity provider prove who the user is, then decide how your app remembers them and how you take that back.
why:
Many government and enterprise apps do not store passwords. They send the user to an identity provider (IdP) and get back a signed statement of who logged in. A design like a Singpass login works this way: the agency's app is the relying party, the IdP authenticates the user, and the app receives an ID token naming the user.

OAuth 2.0 is about delegated access ("this app may call that API"). OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds identity on top: an ID token, a signed JWT that says who the user is, for which app, and until when. The authorization code flow with PKCE is the current recommended flow for web and mobile apps.

After login, the second half of the question is yours: does the app keep a server-side session or hand out JWTs, how long do tokens live, and how do you log someone out everywhere right now?
how:
Authorization code + PKCE, step by step.

  1. The app creates a random state (stops login CSRF), a nonce (ties the ID token to this login) and a code_verifier. It sends the browser to the IdP with code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)).
  2. The user authenticates at the IdP (password, OTP, an app QR scan). The app never sees their credentials.
  3. The IdP redirects back to a pre-registered redirect URI with a one-time, short-lived code and the state.
  4. The backend checks state, then exchanges the code at the token endpoint over a back channel, sending the code_verifier and its own client authentication (a client secret or a signed JWT assertion). A stolen code is useless without the verifier.
  5. The backend verifies the ID token: signature against the IdP's published keys (JWKS), iss, aud equals its client id, exp, and nonce. Then it maps the stable subject (sub) to a local user.

Remembering the user.

  • Server-side session: a random session id in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie, looked up in Redis on each request. Revocation is a delete.
  • Self-contained JWT: any service can verify it with a public key and no lookup. But it is valid until exp, so keep it short (5 to 15 min) and pair it with a refresh token.

Refresh tokens are long-lived, stored server-side or in a secure cookie, and rotated on every use: each refresh returns a new one and invalidates the old. If an old one is used again, assume theft and revoke the whole family.

Revocation. Sessions: delete the row. JWTs: wait for expiry, or check a small denylist of revoked token ids (jti) or a per-user "tokens issued before" timestamp.

flows.name: Login: code + PKCE
flows.desc: The browser carries a code; the backend swaps it for tokens.

steps.note: The user clicks Log in. The app stores state, nonce and a random code_verifier against a short-lived pre-login cookie.
Redirect to the IdP's authorize endpoint with client_id, the registered redirect_uri, scope=openid, state, nonce and code_challenge (SHA-256 of the verifier).
The user authenticates at the IdP, for example by scanning a QR code with an authenticator app. Your app never handles their credentials.
The IdP redirects back with a one-time code that expires in about a minute, plus the same state.
The browser hits /callback?code=...&state=.... Reject it if state does not match: that is a forged login.
Back channel: POST the code, the code_verifier and the app's client authentication to the token endpoint. The IdP checks SHA-256(verifier) equals the challenge.
The IdP returns an ID token (and possibly access and refresh tokens). Verify the signature with the IdP's JWKS, then iss, aud, exp and nonce.
Map the token's stable sub to a local user, creating one on first login. Key on sub, not on an email that can change.
Create a session: a random 128-bit id in Redis with an idle timeout. The browser gets it in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie.

flows.name: Using the session
flows.desc: Cookie to the app, short-lived token to APIs.

steps.note: Each request carries the session cookie. JavaScript cannot read it, which limits what an XSS bug can steal.
One Redis lookup, under 1 ms, confirms the session is still valid. This lookup is what makes instant logout possible.
To call a downstream API, the backend sends a short-lived access token (5 to 15 min). The API verifies it locally with a public key: signature, aud, exp, scopes.
The API answers without calling the IdP. That is the point of a self-contained token, and also why it cannot be revoked early without extra checks.
When the access token expires, the backend uses the refresh token. The IdP returns a new pair and invalidates the old refresh token (rotation).
The user clicks Log out, or an admin disables a compromised account.
Delete the session id. The very next request with that cookie fails. With sessions, revocation is immediate.
Revoke the refresh token so no new access tokens can be minted, and optionally end the IdP session too.
An access token already issued stays valid until exp. Keep that window short, or have APIs check a denylist of revoked token ids for sensitive actions.

tradeoffs.pro: Instant revocation, small cookie, nothing sensitive on the client.
tradeoffs.con: A lookup per request and a shared session store to run and keep available.

tradeoffs.pro: Any service verifies it locally; no central lookup on the hot path.
tradeoffs.con: Cannot be revoked before exp without a denylist; larger on every request; claims go stale.

tradeoffs.option: Short access token + rotated refresh token
tradeoffs.pro: Revocation lag is bounded by the access token TTL; stolen refresh tokens are detectable on reuse.
tradeoffs.con: More moving parts: refresh endpoint, rotation, reuse detection, clock skew.

tradeoffs.option: Tokens in localStorage vs HttpOnly cookie
tradeoffs.pro: localStorage is easy for SPAs to attach as a header.
tradeoffs.con: Any XSS can read localStorage. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by script, but needs SameSite and CSRF care.

numbers: Authorization code lifetime: one use, about 30 to 60 s in practice (the spec recommends at most 10 min).
Access token TTL: 5 to 15 min. That is also the worst-case revocation lag for a JWT with no denylist.
Refresh token / session lifetime: hours to 30 days, with an idle timeout (for example 15 to 30 min for government services).
PKCE code_verifier: 43 to 128 characters of high-entropy randomness; method S256.
Session id: at least 128 bits of randomness. Redis lookup: under 1 ms. A JWT with a few claims: about 0.5 to 1 KB on every request.
say: I'll use OIDC authorization code flow with PKCE: the browser only carries a one-time code, and my backend swaps it for tokens with the verifier and its client credentials.
I verify the ID token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry and nonce, then key the local user on the stable subject, not the email.
For the app I'll use a server-side session in an HttpOnly cookie so logout is immediate; downstream APIs get short-lived access tokens, with refresh tokens rotated on every use.
pitfalls: Skipping state or nonce checks. Without them an attacker can log a victim into the attacker's account, or replay an old ID token.
Trusting a JWT without checking aud, or accepting alg: none or any algorithm the token names. Pin the algorithm and verify every claim.
Long-lived JWTs (days) with no way to revoke them. A stolen token is valid until it expires.
Allowing wildcard or open redirect URIs. The code is then delivered to an attacker's page. Register exact URIs.
Using the implicit flow or putting tokens in URLs. They leak through history, logs and referrer headers; use the code flow with PKCE.

options: An intercepted authorization code being exchanged by someone else
quiz.why: The token endpoint only accepts the code with the original code_verifier, which never left the app. A stolen code alone is useless.

quiz.q: An account is compromised and must lose access immediately. Which design makes that easiest?
options: Server-side sessions: delete the session row
Storing the access token in localStorage
quiz.why: Every request checks the session store, so deleting the row ends access on the next request. A JWT stays valid until it expires unless you add a denylist.

quiz.q: Which ID token check stops a token minted for another app from logging into yours?
quiz.why: The audience says which client the token was issued to. Without the check, any token from the same IdP would be accepted.

quiz.q: A refresh token that was already used once is presented again. What should the server do?
options: Treat it as theft and revoke the whole token family
quiz.why: With rotation each refresh token is single use. Reuse means two parties hold it, so revoke the family and make the user log in again.
